svg.title: Observation, radiosurgery and surgery: the hearing figures of three roads and the rulers each of them uses
svg.desc: Schematic comparing the three management roads for vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), built around the rule that every hearing-preservation figure must carry four labels: grading system, years of follow-up, number of patients and treatment. It opens with the state of the evidence: there is one randomised trial here, comparing radiosurgery with observation, with tumour shrinkage as its primary endpoint, while surgery versus radiosurgery still rests on retrospective cohorts and meta-analyses alone. The first panel is the pillar of the figure, headed "the same ears, the same audiogram, a different grading system": in 156 Danish patients with an intracanalicular vestibular schwannoma followed for nine and a half years on observation alone, serviceable hearing preservation is 34% by AAO-HNS class A to B and 58% by word recognition class 1 to 2 in the very same patients, with "a different ruler = 24 percentage points" written between the two bars and all four labels attached to each. The second panel shows the probability bands from the 2018 Congress of Neurological Surgeons hearing preservation guideline, the one document that puts all three roads in a single table on one definition of serviceable hearing (AAO-HNS class A or B, or Gardner-Robertson class 1 to 2) and one set of time points: radiosurgery 50% to 75% at two years, 50% to 75% at five and 25% to 50% at ten; microsurgery for small to medium sporadic tumours 25% to 50% in all three cells; conservative observation 75% to 100%, 50% to 75% and 25% to 50%. The panel also records that for patients with baseline class A on observation the guideline writes that the ten-year cell has insufficient data to judge; that no pooled number of patients is given because these are bands synthesised from a systematic review rather than a single study; that every recommendation is Level 3 evidence whose verb is "should be counselled that there is a probability of", making them bands for explaining rather than for ranking; and that the only prognostic factor shared by all three roads is that better word recognition and pure-tone threshold before treatment, and a smaller tumour, raise the chance of preservation. The third panel draws the V-REX randomised trial: single-centre, observer-blinded, 100 patients, four years, with tumour volume ratio as the primary endpoint - 0.87 of baseline in the radiosurgery arm (95% confidence interval 0.66 to 1.15) against 1.51 in the wait-and-scan arm, ratio 1.73, p=.002. Beside it sit 26 small squares of which only one is lit and 25 are grey, showing that 25 of the 26 prespecified secondary endpoints showed no difference and that hearing and quality of life are among those 25. Below: 21 patients (42%) in the wait-and-scan arm had radiosurgery within four years because of growth and 28 (56%) ended with no treatment, while 45 (94%) in the radiosurgery arm had no further treatment; and surgery versus radiosurgery has never been randomised. The fourth panel is headed "hearing is falling on both roads" and strikes out two sentences with crosses: "radiosurgery preserves hearing better" and "observation preserves hearing better". Four labelled cards follow: observation, 156 patients, nine and a half years - AAO-HNS class A fell from 19% of patients to 3%, word recognition from 60% to 34%, pure tone from 51 to 72 dB; observation, 636 patients, ten years - 53% had word recognition above 70% at diagnosis and 31% still did at ten years, while 88% of those starting at 100% still had good hearing; observation versus radiosurgery, 237 patients, mean 55 months - loss of serviceable hearing 54/71 (76%) with observation and 34/53 (64%) with radiosurgery, with no statistical difference; and fractionated radiotherapy, 21 patients - 8 (38%) still had serviceable hearing at two years and none at ten years. The last two cards note that the sources write only "serviceable hearing" without stating a grading system. The same panel records what radiosurgery does buy - tumour control and one fewer re-treatment: a systematic review of 24 studies and 4,079 tumours gives 10-year control of 90.93% against 65.24% in 1,959 untreated tumours, an absolute difference of 25.7 percentage points and a number needed to treat of 4, falling to 18.31% and a number needed to treat of 6 in Koos class 1 tumours, while a prospective comparison of 237 patients shows radiosurgery cutting re-treatment to roughly a tenth. The fifth panel draws five measuring sticks of different lengths to show that "tumour control" has no shared definition: a 20% increase in maximum diameter, a 10% increase in volume, a 2 mm increase in maximum diameter, the need for further treatment, and the authors' own definition of "no further treatment", which they acknowledge may underestimate the failure rate. It states that a radiosurgery control rate must not be placed next to a recurrence rate after gross total resection because they are two different rulers, and that whether transient enlargement counts as progression or control depends on each study's threshold and time window; and it gives one fully labelled counter-example - single-session radiosurgery, 1,409 patients, median follow-up six point seven years, pure tone below 50 dB and word recognition above 50%, preservation 59.4%, with the individual ten-year figures scattered between 23% and 58%. The sixth panel sets out the three things worth asking about on the surgical road: the chance of keeping hearing (8 studies, five years or more, AAO-HNS A or B, 310 patients, 60%, in a selected group), the facial nerve (long-term House-Brackmann grade 1 in 228 patients, 94%; persistent facial palsy 3% to 46%; surgical mortality 0.5%; after radiosurgery new facial deficit 1.3% and new trigeminal neuropathy 3.2%) and pain and cerebrospinal fluid leak (2.7% in one surgeon's series of 146 patients). It notes that a meta-analysis of 6,889 patients found no significant difference between three approaches in hearing preservation or facial nerve function, with a non-significant risk ratio for leak, and explains the House-Brackmann scale: grades 1 to 3 the eye still closes on effort, from grade 4 it does not, grade 5 leaves slight movement and grade 6 is complete palsy, with grade 4 as the line that matters. The seventh panel places three citable documents that disagree side by side - the Brazilian Society of Otology guideline favouring surgery for serviceable hearing as a strong recommendation, the Congress of Neurological Surgeons bands pointing the other way, and a systematic review of six retrospective cohorts favouring radiosurgery - under the line "I am not going to pick a side for you"; and below it quality of life, from a meta-analysis of 16 studies and 3,745 patients on the PANQOL scale: observation 69.1 (66.0 to 72.2, n=1,430), radiosurgery 66.9 (62.7 to 71.2, n=864) and microsurgery 61.3 (57.2 to 65.4, n=1,451), with no gap exceeding the minimal clinically important difference and high heterogeneity, plus a prospective comparison of 455 patients followed a mean of four and a half years in which only tinnitus differed, rising 0.8 points with radiosurgery (p=0.005) against a non-significant 0.2 rise with observation and 0.2 fall with surgery. The eighth panel quotes the Taiwanese regulation word for word - "F. A unilateral intracranial cerebellopontine angle acoustic neuroma less than 2.5 cm in width (not including the internal auditory canal)" - and flags beside it that this is a reimbursement threshold and not a treatment threshold, explaining that items 37028B and 37029B are both effective from 1 April 2026, that the indication clause names acoustic neuroma and requires one of six sub-clauses A to F, that 37028B has a general threshold of a diameter under three centimetres or a volume of fifteen cubic centimetres or less while 37029B allows three-dimensional diameters no greater than 3.5 by 3.5 by 3.5 centimetres or a volume of twenty cubic centimetres, that both limit the number of lesions to three, and that every case must be applied for in advance. The figure closes with four questions to take to the clinic: which management are you assessing for my size, location and audiogram; which grading system, how many years, how many patients and which treatment lie behind the preservation rate you quote; if I observe, how often is the scan and what would change the decision; and if I have surgery, what are your own unit's facial nerve and leak figures.

g.text: VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMA - THREE ROADS
Three roads on one table,
and not one cell measured
with the same ruler
This figure does one thing: for vestibular schwannoma
(acoustic neuroma) it puts the four labels that every
hearing-preservation figure needs - grading system,
years of follow-up, number of patients, treatment - next to
the number itself.
It is not a ranking. Hearing falls on all three roads, and in
most comparisons the rate of loss cannot be told apart;
the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying
studies differ, so the data points must not be compared
directly.
There is one randomised trial here, and it compares
stereotactic radiosurgery with observation, with tumour
shrinkage as its primary endpoint; how surgery compares
with radiosurgery still rests on retrospective cohorts and
meta-analyses alone.
The same ears, the same audiogram, a
different grading system
156 Danish patients with an intracanalicular vestibular
schwannoma, observation only, followed for nine and a half
years. Both figures below come from the same patients at the
same follow-up.
AAO-HNS class A to B
grading system
AAO-HNS class A to B
follow-up
nine and a half years
number
treatment
observation only, no treatment
word recognition class 1 to 2
grading system
word recognition class 1 to 2
follow-up
nine and a half years
number
n=156, the same patients
treatment
observation only, no treatment
A different ruler = 24 percentage points
So every hearing-preservation figure has to carry four labels:
grading system, years of follow-up, number of patients,
treatment. If one is missing, discount what you read - every cell
below this one is labelled to that rule.
Three roads in one document: one definition, one
set of time points, one level of evidence
The 2018 guideline of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons is the
only document I found that puts all three roads in the same table.
The gap first: these are bands synthesised from a systematic
review, not a single study, and no pooled number of patients is
given.
stereotactic radiosurgery
2 years
5 years
10 years
microsurgery (small to medium sporadic tumours)
2 years
5 years
10 years
conservative observation
2 years
5 years
10 years
For patients with baseline class A followed by observation, the
guideline writes that the 10-year cell has insufficient data to
judge.
grading system
AAO-HNS class A or B, or Gardner-Robertson class 1
to 2 - shared by all three roads
follow-up
2 years, 5 years and 10 years, shared by all three roads
number
no pooled number of patients is given - these are bands
synthesised from a systematic review
treatment
one column each for radiosurgery, microsurgery and
observation
All of these recommendations are Level 3 evidence, and the verb in
the original is "should be counselled that there is a probability of" -
they are bands for explaining, not for ranking. Only one prognostic
factor is shared by all three roads: the better the word recognition
and pure-tone threshold before treatment, and the smaller the
tumour, the higher the chance of preservation.
That randomised trial does not compare what you
think it compares
V-REX: a single-centre, observer-blinded randomised trial at one
Norwegian hospital. 100 patients with a newly diagnosed small or
medium vestibular schwannoma were randomised to upfront
radiosurgery or to wait-and-scan, and followed for four years.
Primary endpoint: tumour volume ratio
Radiosurgery arm
95% confidence interval 0.66 to 1.15
Wait-and-scan arm
volume at four years relative to baseline
26 prespecified secondary endpoints, 25 with no difference
The lit cell is the direction of the primary endpoint; the 25 grey cells
are the secondary endpoints where no difference was seen - hearing
and quality of life are among those 25.
In the wait-and-scan arm, 21 patients (42%) had radiosurgery
within four years because of growth, and 28 (56%) ended up with
no treatment at all
In the radiosurgery arm, 45 patients (94%) had no further
treatment
Surgery versus radiosurgery has never been randomised.
This cell can only show that radiosurgery shrinks the
tumour; it cannot show that it is better for hearing or
quality of life.
Hearing is falling on both roads
"Radiosurgery preserves hearing better"
"Observation preserves hearing better"
Neither sentence can be written. Hearing falls on both roads, and
in most comparisons the rate of loss cannot be told apart.
Observation
n=156, nine and a half years, observation only
AAO-HNS class A fell from 19% of patients to 3%
Word recognition fell from 60% to 34%
Pure-tone threshold rose from 51 to 72 dB
Observation
n=636, ten years, word recognition
53% had word recognition above 70% at diagnosis; 31% still did
at ten years
Of those starting at 100% word recognition, 88% still had good
hearing at ten years
Observation vs radiosurgery
n=237, mean 55 months, serviceable hearing
Loss of serviceable hearing: observation 54/71 (76%),
radiosurgery 34/53 (64%)
No statistical difference
The source writes only "serviceable hearing" and does not
state which grading system
Fractionated radiotherapy
n=21, two years and ten years, serviceable hearing
Of the 21 patients with serviceable hearing before treatment, 8
(38%) still had it at two years
At ten years, nobody in the radiotherapy group had
serviceable hearing
The source writes only "serviceable hearing" and does not
state which grading system
What radiosurgery buys is two other things: tumour
control, and one fewer re-treatment
A systematic review of 24 studies and 4,079 tumours:
10-year tumour control 90.93%, against 65.24% in 1,959
untreated tumours - an absolute difference of 25.7
percentage points and a number needed to treat of 4
In the Koos class 1 tumours of that same review, the
absolute difference is only 18.31% and the number needed
to treat 6
A prospective comparison (n=237): radiosurgery cut the
chance of re-treatment to roughly a tenth
"Tumour control" has no shared definition in this
literature
A meta-analysis of 23 studies laid out how each study defined
tumour progression. Every stick below is a different length,
because they were never the same ruler.
a 20% increase in maximum diameter
a 10% increase in volume
a 2 mm increase in maximum diameter
the need for further treatment
in the end the authors had to define their own - "no further treatment" -
and acknowledged it may underestimate the failure rate
Do not put a radiosurgery control rate next to a recurrence
rate after gross total resection - they are two different
rulers. Whether transient enlargement counts as
progression or as control also depends on each study's
threshold and time window.
In that same meta-analysis the hearing figure does carry all
four labels: single-session radiosurgery, 1,409 patients,
median follow-up of six point seven years, pure tone below 50
dB and word recognition above 50%, preservation 59.4%; the
ten-year figures of the individual studies are scattered
between 23% and 58%.
On the surgical road, three things are worth
asking about
The approach anatomy is not yours to worry about: a
meta-analysis of 6,889 patients comparing three approaches found
no significant difference in hearing preservation or facial nerve
function, and the risk ratio for cerebrospinal fluid leak was not
significant either.
The chance of keeping hearing
Patients selected for hearing-preservation surgery, 8 studies,
followed five years or more:
long-term serviceable hearing (AAO-HNS A or B, 310 patients)
This is a selected group, not everyone who needs an operation
The facial nerve
Long-term House-Brackmann grade 1 facial function (228
patients) 94%
Persistent facial palsy ranges from 3% to 46%; surgical
mortality 0.5%
After radiosurgery, new facial nerve deficit (worse than
grade 2) 1.3% and new trigeminal neuropathy 3.2%
Pain and cerebrospinal fluid leak
Leak was 2.7% in one surgeon's series of 146 patients
The risk ratio for leak did not differ significantly between the
three approaches
Facial nerve results are reported on the House-Brackmann
scale: at grades 1 to 3 the eye still closes completely on
effort; from grade 4 it does not; grade 5 leaves only slight
movement; grade 6 is complete palsy. Grade 4 is the line that
matters - once the eye will not close, eye care becomes a
daily task.
Three citable documents point in different
directions
Brazilian Society of Otology guideline
surgery is superior to radiotherapy for preserving serviceable
hearing (strong recommendation)
The probability bands of the Congress of Neurological
Surgeons
point the other way
A systematic review of six retrospective cohorts
favours radiosurgery
I am not going to pick a side for you.
Seen through quality of life, the three roads differ less than the
weight of the decision suggests.
Observation
95% confidence interval 66.0 to 72.2, n=1,430
Radiosurgery
Microsurgery
A meta-analysis of 16 studies and 3,745 patients using PANQOL, the
disease-specific scale for vestibular schwannoma, measured at least
a year after intervention or diagnosis; no gap between the three
groups exceeds the minimal clinically important difference, and
heterogeneity between studies is high. In another prospective
comparison (455 patients, mean follow-up four and a half years, a 0
to 10 scale) only tinnitus differed: the radiosurgery group rose by 0.8
points (p=0.005), while the observation group rose 0.2 and the
surgical group fell 0.2, neither significantly.
What the Taiwanese regulation actually says
"F. A unilateral intracranial cerebellopontine angle
acoustic neuroma less than 2.5 cm in width (not
including the internal auditory canal)."
This is a reimbursement threshold, not a treatment
threshold.
The National Health Insurance fee schedule carries two
stereotactic radiosurgery items (37028B and 37029B, the current
versions both effective 1 April 2026), and the indication clause
names acoustic neuroma word for word while requiring one of six
sub-clauses A to F to be met at the same time; clause F is the one
specific to acoustic neuroma. Each item has its own general
threshold: for 37028B a diameter under three centimetres or a
volume of fifteen cubic centimetres or less, for 37029B
three-dimensional diameters no greater than 3.5 x 3.5 x 3.5
centimetres or a volume of twenty cubic centimetres, and both
limit the number of lesions to three. Every case must be applied
for in advance. The literature does not agree on where the line
sits, and this clause is yet another ruler.
Take these four sentences unchanged to a surgeon
and to an otologist, and ask each of them
Given my size, my location and this audiogram, which
management are you assessing?
The preservation rate you are quoting - which grading
system, how many years, how many patients, which
treatment?
If I observe, how often is the scan and what would change
the decision?
If I have surgery, what are your own unit's facial nerve
and leak figures?
Schematic, redrawn from the V-REX randomised trial (Dhayalan 2023),
the 2018 Congress of Neurological Surgeons hearing preservation
guideline, Kirchmann 2017, Stangerup 2008, Breivik 2013, Rasmussen
2012, Guy 2025, Balossier 2023, Garcia-Torrico 2025, Foo 2026, the 2023
Brazilian Society of Otology guideline, Pruijn 2026, Khandalavala 2025 and
the National Health Insurance fee schedule, rather than reproduced from
their figures; the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies
differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
